newsitem.title: USA: U.S. September consumer credit fell $2.6 billion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. September consumer credit fell $2.6 billion.

text.p: U.S. consumer installment credit fell $2.6 billion in September at a 2.7 percent annual rate, the Federal Reserve said Thursday, after rising a revised $5 billion in August at a 5.2 percent annual rate.
The Fed said it was the first decline in monthly consumer credit in more than three years, since May 1993 when it fell $200 million at a 0.3 percent rate.
Previously, the Fed said August consumer credit outstanding had risen by $3.3 billion but it revised that upward.
The drop in September consumer credit was sharply contrary to Wall Street analysts' forecasts for a $5.6 billion increase in outstanding credit instead of a decline.
Auto credit decreased $1 billion in September at a 3.1 percent annual rate, after rising $700 million at a 2.2 percent annual rate in August.
But revolving or credit-card debt rose in September by $1 billion at a 2.6 percent annual rate, compared with a $2.5 billion August rise at a 6.7 percent annual rate.
Credit-card debt was the only major category that posted an increase in outstanding balances in September.

Other credit, which includes consumer bank loans but not real estate mortgages, fell by $2.6 billion at a 9.1 percent annual rate in September after rising $1.8 billion at a 6.3 percent rate in August, the Fed said.
Before seasonal adjustment, total outstanding consumer credit in September was $1.18 trillion, up from $1.17 trillion in August and up from $1.08 trillion in September 1995.
